chapman_shrewsbury.text: Chapbooks, friend. Darwin bought one here, I'm fairly sure. Could have been a pie.

rail_guard.text: Shrewsbury Station, done up in mock Tudor in 1848 to match the black-and-white town. Part of it is built out over the river. Lovely, as long as you don't drop your ticket.
Trains to everywhere you have been. You need a Rail Pass, and if you say Shrewsbury wrong the barrier says it back to you.

then.text: Shrows. Shrews. The Wrekin doesn't care and neither do the ponies. We've agreed to disagree, loudly, every Saturday.
Well? What did they say? ... The Wrekin walker says Shrows, and the pony warden says Shrews. A draw!
That's how it's always been. Shrewsbury School, the old families and half the town say Shrows. The other half, and most visitors, say Shrews. Even the dictionaries give both.
Here, have some cakes for your trouble. Shrewsbury cakes. However you say it.
Ask the walker on top of the Wrekin, east of here, then the pony warden on the Long Mynd, south. Neutral ground, both of them.

else.text: It's SHROWS-bury. Rhymes with 'throws'. My family has said it that way since the Tudors.
She says SHROOS-bury, like the animal. We've argued about it since the coronation. Not this one. The one before.
You look impartial. Go and ask the Wrekin walker, east of here past the Iron Bridge road, and the pony warden up on the Long Mynd. Bring back their verdicts.

shr_shrews.text: SHROOS-bury. Like the animal, a shrew. Spelt like it, said like it. Simple.
He'll tell you the posh school says Shrows. They do. That's half the problem.

shr_coracle.text: A coracle is a round little boat of willow and hide, or calico and tar these days, light enough to carry on your back. Folk fished the Severn from them for centuries.
When Shrewsbury Town played down at the Gay Meadow by the river, a coracle man used to paddle out and fetch the footballs that sailed over the stand. Best job in football.

then.text: Long grass in the Quarry, logs by the river, and up on the Long Mynd. Squibbets love a damp log. Mind they don't squirt you.
Beetles for the library? Darwin's old school, I know. Look in the long grass in the Quarry, south of St Chad's, and up on the Long Mynd past Kingsland Bridge.
The Squibbet is the one with the shiny shell. Pick it up and it'll squirt. Young Charles found that out the hard way.

else.text: The Dingle was a quarry pit once. Now it's the prettiest hole in England. Mind the dahlias; they've been entered for August.
If you're after beetles, turn over a log by the river. Gently, and put it back.

shr_cadfael.text: Brother Cadfael was a Welsh monk who had been a crusader and a sailor before he settled down to grow herbs at Shrewsbury Abbey and solve murders. Twenty books of them.
The books are set in the 1130s and 40s, during the war between Stephen and Matilda. Ellis Peters was the pen name of Edith Pargeter, a Shropshire writer.

shr_cakes.text: Shrewsbury cakes are not cakes. They are crisp, buttery biscuits with a hint of lemon and a scalloped edge, and they've been made here since at least the 1500s.
In the old days they were a famous present to send off by coach. They arrived in crumbs, and everybody said that was the authentic way.

shr_drover.text: Welsh drovers came over this bridge with their cattle and their wool for hundreds of years. The town got rich on Welsh wool, cloth and the trade along the Severn.
In Welsh the town is Amwythig. Write that down. There'll be a test.

shr_rower.text: EASY OAR! Sorry. Habit. The school's rowers train on this stretch of the Severn. The river loops so tightly round the town you can row for miles and never get anywhere.
Rowing on a river with a current is all about the timing. Rather like getting a word in at a Shrewsbury dinner party.
